splash.heading: What type of learner are you?
splash.subheading: Take the test to see what type of learner you are and what that meant we considered when designing Money&Me

questions.context: You've signed up for a new learning app.
questions.question: What do you do first?

options.text: Skip straight to the first test to see how I do
Browse the topics and pick the one that looks interesting
Check what badges and rewards are available and then choose

questions.context: You earn a badge for completing a module. A few months later, the content gets updated.
questions.question: What happens?

options.text: I go back and do it, I want the knowledge to stay current
I still have the badge, so I'm good
I skim the update but don't retake the test

questions.context: You're halfway through a module and realise you already know most of this.
questions.question: You...

options.text: Keep reading anyway, you might learn something new
Jump to the knowledge check and see if you can pass it cold
Close and come back when there's something more interesting
Finish it properly still, completion matters

questions.context: Your employer sends a notification: three new modules added.
questions.question: You...

options.text: Open the link and immediately learn it
Check the link, if it's relevant, I'll do it
Open all three, skim to find the quickest one to complete

ideal.name: Ideal player
ideal.desc: You engage with content properly, complete knowledge checks, and actually come back when things update. You're exactly who the platform was designed for.
ideal.designImplications: Designing for you is the easy part. The real challenge was making sure the platform didn't punish everyone else for not being you.

speedrunner.name: Speed runner
speedrunner.desc: Tests first, content never. You've found the most efficient path to a badge and you're not apologising for it. Honestly, fair enough.
speedrunner.designImplications: Speed runners taught us that if knowledge checks can be gamed, they will be. We had to design reward logic that still delivered value even when the content got skipped.

learner.name: Deep learner
learner.desc: You're here for the knowledge, not the gamification. Badges don't motivate you — understanding does. The platform had to make sure you didn't feel penalised for ignoring the parts you didn't care about.
learner.designImplications: You validated our decision to make the experience non-linear. Forcing a learner through gamification they don't want is the fastest way to lose them.

ghost.name: Ghost
ghost.desc: You showed up, collected some badges, then quietly disappeared. New content came and went without you. The platform doesn't know you've moved on — but you have.
ghost.designImplications: Ghosts are the hardest archetype to design for, because they've already left. Re-engagement had to feel like an invitation, not a guilt trip.

timedout.name: Timed-out
timedout.desc: You did everything right — once. But the world moved on and your knowledge didn't come with it. You carry badges for things that have since been updated.
timedout.designImplications: This archetype pushed us to think about knowledge decay, not just knowledge acquisition. A badge shouldn't mean 'I knew this once'.

scoring.notes: In a tie, the archetype with the highest score wins. If scores are equal, the first alphabetically in the scores object wins — consider whether this edge case needs a dedicated tiebreaker question.
